title: The Guinness Book of Records
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the Guinness Book of World Records, starting with its origin in 1950s Ireland when Sir Hugh Beaver, managing director of Guinness brewery, failed to find an answer to the fastest European game bird and conceived a pub reference book. They cover the McWhirter twins (Norris and Ross) who compiled the first edition published in 1955, its sales growth, later ownership changes (Guinness sold it to Guiness-era company Gulane, then the Jim Pattison Group), the 1975 murder of Ross McWhirter by IRA-linked gunmen, the record-submission criteria and guidelines, adjudicators and their rules, GWR Consultancy's paid record-making for companies, controversy over Turkmenistan's dictator, criticism from former staff, and fun records such as Diana Armstrong's long fingernails and Ashrita Furman's record count. The episode closes with listener mail about wind power in Denton, Texas.
topics: Denton Texas wind power listener mail

segments.title: Opening banter and Chin Wag plug
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the show, Josh plugs his guest appearance on the Chin Wag podcast with Paul Giamatti and Stephen Asma, and they transition to the topic.

segments.title: Childhood memories of the book and listener suggestion
segments.summary: The hosts recall reading the Guinness book as kids, remember iconic pictures such as the longest fingernails and the McWhirter brothers and the tall man, and credit listener Mallory Stafford for the episode suggestion.

segments.title: Sir Hugh Beaver and the origin of the book
segments.summary: Sir Hugh Beaver, managing director of Guinness, missed a shot at a golden plover in Ireland in 1950 and could not settle the fastest game bird question in a reference book, leading him to propose a pub reference book of facts.

segments.title: McWhirter twins and early research
segments.summary: Beaver turned to Norris and Ross McWhirter, identical twins who ran a fact-checking agency, forming Guinness Superlatives in London. They spent months sourcing records from experts, finding that experts sometimes got facts wrong, such as a claimed fly speed.

segments.title: First edition, sales, and early reputation for accuracy
segments.summary: The first edition appeared August 27, 1955, with about 4,000 entries, was given out at pubs, and sold 187,000 copies by Christmas. Total sales are said to be about 150 million. The McWhirters emphasized accuracy and family-friendly content.

segments.title: Fastest game birds and Ross McWhirter's murder
segments.summary: The hosts settle the fastest European game bird debate, then describe how Ross McWhirter, a political activist, offered a reward for information on IRA bombers and was shot dead in 1975 by members of the Balcombe Street gang. Norris continued as editor until 1986.

segments.title: Ownership changes and company today
segments.summary: Guinness sold the record business to Gulane, which later sold it to the Jim Pattison Group. The company expanded beyond the book into museums and attractions and now has offices in London, Dubai, Tokyo, New York and Beijing with about 400 staff.

segments.title: Record submission criteria and guidelines
segments.summary: Records must be measurable, breakable, standardizable, verifiable, single-variable, universal, and substantially different from existing records. Guidelines can run dozens of pages and many applicants drop out. About 50,000 applicants yearly and roughly 2,000 records added; success rate about 5 to 10 percent.

segments.title: Brandon's piggyback ride record attempt
segments.summary: The hosts describe their webmaster Brandon, who briefly held the Guinness record for fastest 400 meter piggyback ride with a friend before it was broken quickly, so his certificate was never issued.

segments.title: Prohibited record attempts
segments.summary: Records cannot endanger others, involve pets, excessive eating, drinking, illegal acts, or unsuitable activities involving children; minors need parental sign-up. Dangerous records like longest kiss and dance marathons were dropped, as was invasive surgery.

segments.title: Adjudicators and their rules
segments.summary: About ninety adjudicators travel the world to oversee attempts, following strict rules: branded jacket, no socializing or eating with attempters, media training. Craig Glenday described a Moscow concrete-pouring attempt where the adjudicator declared success to get out safely and revoked it later.

segments.title: Remote verification and paid fast-track consultancy
segments.summary: Videos alone are insufficient; live non-family witnesses are required. Paying for fast-track adjudicator visits and GWR Consultancy's paid brand record services are controversial, though attempts are legitimate and about half of revenue comes from companies.

segments.title: Turkmenistan controversy and criticism of the company
segments.summary: Guinness worked with Turkmenistan's dictator Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedov, who sought records such as highest density of white marble-clad buildings, drawing criticism. Former PR head Anna Nicholas and Alistair McWhirter said the company has lost intellectual integrity.

segments.title: Closing reflections on the company's survival
segments.summary: Chuck says Guinness World Records survives in the internet age, still sells about a million books a year, and keeps Norris and Ross's principles of accuracy.

segments.title: Fun records: fingernails, four-leaf clovers, and Ashrita Furman
segments.summary: Diana Armstrong holds the longest fingernails record at over 42 feet after not cutting them since 1997. George Kaminski set a four-leaf clover collection record in prison. Ashrita Furman holds the most Guinness records, over 700.

segments.title: Listener mail: wind power in Denton, Texas
segments.summary: Listener Ben from Denton, Texas writes about the city's municipal utility, renewable energy push, and Texas's grid, and the hosts look up the University of North Texas mascot.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts invite listener emails and sign off.
